commitResults.messageTitle: Rename chatbot to Ted and greet the user on startup
commitResults.messageBody:
Rename the Duke class to Ted (with a matching ASCII banner) so the
project uses its own product name rather than the template's default,
updating both READMEs to match.

Implement the Level-0 requirement: the chatbot now prints its banner,
greets the user, and immediately says goodbye, with each section
separated by a horizontal line. The divider is extracted into a
printLine() helper rather than repeating the literal string, since
every future command response will need the same separator.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Fill in the student profile
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the [to be filled] placeholders with the actual experience level
and IDE, so AI assistants working in this repo can pitch explanations at
the right level instead of guessing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Ted printed a greeting and exited immediately, so there was no way to
interact with it. Add a read-print loop so the user can enter commands.

Each line entered is echoed back between horizontal rules, and the
command 'bye' ends the conversation. Input is trimmed so that stray
whitespace does not stop 'bye' from matching, and the loop also stops on
end-of-input so that piping a script into the program exits cleanly
rather than throwing NoSuchElementException.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Ted.java: Add task storage and the list command
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted previously echoed each input straight back and forgot it. He now
remembers what the user types and can recall it on demand:

* Non-command input is stored and acknowledged with "added: <task>".
* The "list" command prints the stored tasks, numbered from 1.

Tasks are held in a fixed-size String[100] with a separate taskCount,
which is sufficient because this increment caps the task count at 100.
An ArrayList would be the natural replacement once that cap is lifted,
but the array keeps the code simple for now.

Adding beyond the 100-task limit reports the failure instead of writing
past the end of the array, so a dropped task is never silent, and "list"
on an empty task list says so rather than printing an empty response.

Also fixed the farewell, which printed with only a trailing separator
line, so that it is bracketed on both sides like every other response.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Tasks previously had no state beyond their description, so there was no
way to record progress. A parallel boolean[] now tracks the done status
of each task, and "mark <number>" sets it.

The list output changes to show a status icon per task ("1.[X] read
book"), which is the format the later increments build on.

A mistyped task number is a normal part of using a chatbot, so
parseTaskIndex reports missing, non-numeric, and out-of-range numbers
instead of letting the exception escape and end the conversation.

Keeping the description and its done status in two parallel arrays is
deliberately awkward at this step; the next commits introduce a Task
class that bundles them together.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

A task marked done by mistake could not be corrected without restarting
Ted. "unmark <number>" now reverses the done status.

Marking and unmarking differ only in the flag they store and the wording
they print, so both route through one setTaskDone method rather than
duplicating the task-number lookup and its error handling.

"unmark" is tested before "mark" when dispatching, because "unmark 2"
would otherwise have to be distinguished from a mark command by a more
fragile check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a Task class to represent tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
A task's description and its done status were held in two parallel
arrays, which only stayed in step because every write updated both by
hand. A Task object now owns both, so a task cannot lose its status.

Task also overrides toString, which moves the display format next to the
data it formats and lets a task be printed wherever it is needed. This
replaces Ted's formatTask helper, which had to reach into both arrays.

Task is a separate file rather than a nested class because the later
increments give it subclasses for the different kinds of task.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Todo, Deadline and Event task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Every task was the same shape, so a due date or a time span had to be
buried in the description as plain text. Ted now understands three
commands that create three kinds of task, each shown with its own type
icon: todo, deadline (/by) and event (/from, /to).

Task becomes abstract and gains an abstract getTypeIcon, because a task
with no kind is no longer something the user can create. Deadline and
Event extend toString by calling super and appending their own detail,
so the shared "[icon][status] description" format is defined once.

Dates stay free text, as this increment allows; "no idea :-p" is as
valid as "Sunday". Converting them to real dates comes later.

Adding a task now reports the task and the resulting task count, which
is what the later delete command will echo too.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle invalid user input with a TedException
commitResults.messageBody:
Bad input was handled inconsistently: some cases printed a message from
deep inside a helper, some returned a sentinel -1 the caller had to
remember to check, and an empty todo was stored as a blank task.

Every recoverable problem is now reported by throwing a TedException,
caught in one place in the main loop. Detecting code says what went
wrong, the loop decides how to show it, and no failure can slip past a
forgotten sentinel check. The exception is checked, because each of
these is a normal part of a conversation rather than a bug.

Messages name the specific problem and show a working example, so the
user can correct the command without consulting a guide.

Dispatch now splits the command word from its argument instead of using
startsWith, which also fixes "todos something" being silently accepted
as a todo named "s something".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the delete command and store tasks in an ArrayList
commitResults.messageBody:
A task added by mistake could not be removed. "delete <number>" now
removes one and echoes it, since after it is gone the user has no other
way to confirm the number they typed was the one they meant.

Deleting from the fixed-size array would have meant shifting every later
task down by hand and keeping a separate count in step, so tasks move to
an ArrayList, which closes the gap itself and reports its own size. The
100-task cap and its "list is full" error disappear with it, as the list
grows as needed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Represent commands with an enum instead of String constants
commitResults.messageBody:
The command words were eight loose String constants matched by a switch
over raw strings, so a typo in a constant or a case label would compile
and only show up as a command that silently stopped working. The list of
keywords in the "I don't recognise that" message was a ninth copy that
had to be edited by hand whenever a command was added, and had already
drifted once.

A Command enum now owns each keyword and looks it up in one place, so
the compiler checks every use, the switch reads as a list of commands
rather than of strings, and the message shown to a confused user is
built from the commands themselves.

Blank input is now ignored rather than answered with a complaint about
an empty command word.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Tasks exist only in memory, so exiting Ted loses the user's task list.

Let's load tasks during startup and save after each list mutation. Store
them in a human-readable format, with escaping so free-form text can
round-trip without changing field boundaries.

Ignore generated class and runtime data files so local runs do not
pollute commits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store deadline and event times as date-times
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and Event keep their times as free text, so Ted cannot tell
"2/12/2019 1800" from "no idea :-p".

That rules out anything that reasons about time, such as ordering tasks
or listing what is due on a given day, and lets nonsense through.

Let's store the times as java.time.LocalDateTime, read in d/M/yyyy HHmm
form and shown back as "2 Dec 2019, 6:00 pm". Times Ted cannot read are
reported as a TedException, and an event that ends before it starts is
now rejected.

The save file uses ISO-8601 rather than the display format, so it stays
unambiguous and independent of how Ted happens to print dates.

Brings in Level 8: deadlines and events store their times as
LocalDateTime instead of free text.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui, TaskList and Storage responsibilities
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted prints the banner, reads the keyboard, holds the task list, checks
task numbers and writes the save file.

One class holding all of that means a change to any one of them edits
the same file, and none of it can be exercised without a terminal.

Let's split those responsibilities out:
* Ui owns the Scanner and every System.out
* TaskList owns the tasks and the rule that a task number must point at
  a real task
* Storage takes its file path from the constructor and reports failures
  as a TedException instead of printing them

Storage taking a path rather than hard-coding one lets a later test
point it at a scratch file instead of the real save file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser: read user input into Command objects
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted routes every command itself, through a switch that calls one private
method per command word, and those methods do the reading and the work
in one go.

Every new command therefore means another branch in that switch and
another method on an already large class, and nothing that reads user
input can be tested apart from the code that acts on it.

Let's,
* add a Command class with one subclass per kind of command, each
  carrying out its own work through execute(tasks, ui, storage)
* move all input reading into a new Parser, which returns the Command
  the user asked for
* rename the old Command enum to CommandType, since it now names the
  kinds of command rather than being one

Splitting reading from doing means a command is only built once its
details make sense, so the command classes need no input checking, and
Parser can be tested without a keyboard or a save file.

Brings in A-MoreOOP: Ui, TaskList, Storage, Parser and the Command
classes are now separate, leaving Ted to wire them together.

All seventeen classes sit in the default package, so src/main/java is a
flat list in which nothing says which classes belong together.

The default package also cannot be imported from elsewhere, and the list
only gets harder to read as more classes are added.

Let's group them into three packages under src/main/java:
* ted for the app itself: Ted, Ui, Parser, Storage, TedException
* ted.task for the tasks and the list holding them
* ted.command for the commands and the keywords naming them

Splitting by role rather than keeping one ted package makes the
boundaries between talking, storing and doing visible in the folder
structure. Task.SAVE_FIELD_SEPARATOR becomes public because Storage,
which splits save lines on it, now sits outside ted.task.

Brings in A-Packages: the classes are grouped into ted, ted.task and
ted.command.

Brings in the Gradle wrapper and build.gradle, so the project can be
built, run and tested with one command on any machine.

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Point Gradle at this project
commitResults.messageBody:
The build file merged in from add-gradle-support names seedu.duke.Duke
as the main class and duke.jar as the JAR to build.

Neither exists here, so `gradlew run` fails on a project whose entry
point is ted.Ted.

Let's set mainClass to ted.Ted and the shadowJar name to ted.jar.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for Parser, TaskList, Storage and Task
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing in the project is covered by an automated test, so every change
has to be checked by typing commands at the chatbot and reading what
comes back.

That is slow, easy to skip, and quietly misses the cases a person would
not think to type, such as a save file someone edited by hand.

Let's add 57 JUnit tests over the four classes whose failures would hurt
most:
* ParserTest, since Parser is where malformed input is caught
* TaskListTest, for the bounds checking behind every task number
* StorageTest, for the save-and-load round trip, writing in a @TempDir
  so the tests never touch the real save file
* TaskTest, for the display and save formats

Writing them turned up one bug: the default date resolver silently
rounded 31/2/2019 down to 28 Feb, so Ted accepted a date the user could
not have meant. Parser now uses the strict resolver, which rejects it.

Brings in A-JUnit: 57 tests over Parser, TaskList, Storage and Task, plus
the strict date resolver those tests prompted.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the packages and the remaining overrides
commitResults.messageBody:
Most classes and methods carry a Javadoc header, but the three packages
have none, several overrides in ted.command and ted.task are undocumented,
and `gradlew javadoc` reports five warnings about default constructors.

A reader opening the generated docs therefore meets three unexplained
packages, and the warnings hide any real problem that appears later.

Let's,
* add package-info.java for ted, ted.task and ted.command, each saying
  what the package is for and how its classes fit together
* document the execute() overrides, isExit() and the getTypeIcon()
  overrides
* give Ui, Command, ListCommand and ExitCommand documented constructors,
  and make Parser's private since it is used through static methods only

`gradlew javadoc` now runs clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project has no written coding standard, so nothing says which
conventions the code follows or which ones new code should follow.

Without that, style drifts as the code grows, and neither a reader nor an
AI assistant working in this repository has anything to check against.

Let's adopt the SE-EDU Java coding standard at the intermediate level:
* record it in AGENTS.md, along with the SE-EDU Git commit conventions,
  so future code and commits are held to both
* move the two trailing end-of-line comments onto their own line above
  the code they explain

The rest of the code already complies: a sweep for tabs, over-long lines,
wildcard imports, misgrouped imports and brace-less bodies found nothing
else to change.

A user with a long list can only look for a task by reading the whole
list and picking it out by eye.

That gets harder with every task added, and the list is the only view
Ted offers.

Let's add `find <keyword>`, which shows the tasks whose description
contains the keyword:

    find book
    Here are the matching tasks in your list:
    1.[T][X] read book
    2.[D][X] return book (by: 6 Jun 2026, 6:00 pm)

The search ignores case and matches part of a word, since a user
searching for "book" should not have to remember whether they typed
"Book" or "bookshop" when adding the task.

The matches are numbered from 1 as their own list, so those numbers are
not the ones to pass to mark or delete.

Brings in A-JavaDoc: package-info for the three packages, headers on the
remaining overrides, and a warning-free `gradlew javadoc`.

Brings in A-CodingStandard: the SE-EDU Java coding standard and Git commit
conventions are recorded in AGENTS.md, and the code complies.

Brings in Level 9: a find command that shows the tasks whose description
contains a keyword.

commitResults.messageTitle: FindCommand: Add the missing header comment
commitResults.messageBody:
FindCommand was written on branch-Level-9, in parallel with the JavaDoc
pass on branch-A-JavaDoc, so its execute() override missed that pass.

Every other execute() override carries a one-line header saying what the
command does and whether it saves.

Let's give FindCommand the same, so the command classes read alike.

The coding standard this project follows is only checked by eye at
the moment. Style slips are easy to miss during review, and they are
noticed late, when the code has already been merged.

Let's add the Gradle CheckStyle plugin, using the rule set from the
AddressBook Level 3 project because it is the configuration that
matches the SE-EDU Java coding standard. Wiring it into the build
means `gradlew check` fails on a violation, so style is enforced by
the build rather than by the reviewer.

The first run reported eight violations, fixed here:

* Parser declared its private constructor above the static
  constants. DeclarationOrder wants statics first, so the
  constructor moves below them.
* Four assertions in ParserTest wrapped so that a lambda's `(`
  opened the next line. SeparatorWrap wants a wrapped `(` to stay
  on the previous line, and each of these fits on one line within
  the 120-column limit anyway.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Ted only talks over a terminal, which means the app has to be started
from a command line and its replies scroll away with everything else
in the shell.

Let's give Ted a JavaFX window, built the way the SE-EDU tutorial
describes: the layout in FXML, the behaviour in a controller, and the
JavaFX libraries taken from Maven Central for all three OSes so the
jar is not tied to the machine that built it.

Ui no longer prints; it builds up a reply that flush() hands back.
That is what lets one chatbot serve both interfaces -- the terminal
prints the reply between its divider lines, and the window puts the
same text in a dialog box, where the dividers would be clutter. Ted
gains getResponse for the GUI to call a message at a time, while run()
keeps the text interface working, which is still the easier of the two
to test.

The entry point is a separate Launcher class. JavaFX will not start
from a class that extends Application when its libraries are on the
classpath rather than the module path, which is how this project
depends on them.

The bye command is kept rather than leaving the window close button as
the only way out, since quitting by typing matches the rest of the
app's command-driven feel. The window closes a moment after the
goodbye so the message can be read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Use varargs where the argument count varies
commitResults.messageBody:
Two places build up a result from a number of pieces that is fixed per
caller but differs between callers, and both spell that out by hand.

Each Task subclass assembles its own save line, repeating the escaping
and separator placement that the base class already knows how to do.
Let's replace toSavePrefix with toSaveLine(String...), so a subclass
names only the fields it adds -- none for a todo, by for a deadline,
from and to for an event -- and the escaping and separators stay in
one place.

Ui called show once per line, so a two-line reply read as two
unrelated statements. Let's make show take varargs, so each reply is
one call whose arguments are the lines the user will see.

Both are cases where the count varies by caller and every argument
means the same kind of thing, which is what varargs are for. Passing
an explicit array, or overloading for one and two extra fields, would
say the same thing with more ceremony.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
